term.name: Stream cipher
term.short: A stream cipher encrypts data by combining plaintext with a pseudorandom keystream generated from a secret key and nonce.
term.meta_title: Stream Cipher — Definition and Security | CiphersOnline
term.meta_description: Learn how stream ciphers generate keystream, why reusing a key and nonce is dangerous, and why encryption must also authenticate the data.

body.title: Definition
body.html: A stream cipher generates a pseudorandom keystream from a secret key and usually a nonce, then combines it with plaintext—commonly using XOR—to produce ciphertext. Decryption combines the same keystream with the ciphertext. ChaCha20 is a modern example.

body.title: Keystream reuse
body.html: The same keystream must never encrypt two different messages. Reusing a key and nonce can expose the XOR of the plaintexts and allow both messages to be recovered. Protocols therefore assign a unique nonce to every encryption under a key.

body.title: Integrity
body.html: A basic stream cipher provides confidentiality but does not detect modification: changing a ciphertext bit predictably changes the plaintext. Modern systems use an authenticated construction such as ChaCha20-Poly1305 and verify its tag before releasing data.

faq.question: Is a stream cipher the same as a block cipher?
faq.answer: No. A native stream cipher generates keystream, while a block cipher permutes fixed-size blocks. Some block-cipher modes behave like stream ciphers.

faq.question: Can a stream-cipher nonce be public?
faq.answer: Usually yes. It must be unique for the key; secrecy is normally not required.

faq.question: Why is key-and-nonce reuse catastrophic?
faq.answer: It repeats the keystream, canceling it when ciphertexts are compared and exposing a direct relationship between the plaintexts.
